paragraphs.text:
On a hot morning on the east coast of Kythera, a narrow strip of sea glimmers below a sky so bright that the eye can barely endure it.
The place looks barren, almost forsaken, yet its stony surface preserves a dense record of human movement across thousands of years.

figures.label: Figure 1.1
figures.caption: A view over eastern Kythera and Avlemonas. The image makes clear how a seemingly spare coastal landscape could serve as a long-used anchorage and a crossroads of movement.

paragraphs.text:
Archaeologists working there were collecting battered fragments of pottery from a site about three thousand five hundred years old.
The finds were modest in scale, but they revealed that this harsh corner of the island had once belonged to the wider Minoan world.
People here cooked, stored goods, and probably worked a difficult landscape with terraces, while a nearby open-air shrine and the port of Kastri tied the area to larger networks of power, ritual, and exchange.

figures.label: Figure 1.1
figures.caption: The eastern coast of Kythera seen from above. It helps situate the Bronze Age activity, the nearby harbor, and the small but strategic coastal world described in the text.

timeline.label: Neolithic Kythera
timeline.caption: Earlier small communities on Kythera form the deeper background behind the later Bronze Age activity.

timeline.label: Minoan palatial period
timeline.caption: The mature Cretan horizon in which Kythera could function as part of a wider Minoan network.

timeline.label: Mycenaean Aegean
timeline.caption: The later Bronze Age successor horizon that followed the peak Minoan phase.

timeline.label: Kastri on Kythera
timeline.caption: The port-town of Kastri marks the phase of strong Cretan influence described in this paragraph.

paragraphs.text:
The traces went further back still.
Small scatters of pottery and obsidian showed that people had been living or passing through here in the Neolithic, already linked by sea to Melos, the nearest source of that volcanic glass.
An even earlier arrowhead hinted at hunting or fishing parties in the seventh millennium BC.
Seen in this longer perspective, Kythera was not a lonely edge at all, but one station within a corridor running between the Peloponnese and Crete.

figures.label: Figure 1.1
figures.caption: The same Kytheran coastline viewed as part of a wider maritime corridor. The point is not scenery alone, but the island's position between larger lands and sea routes.

timeline.label: Mesolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: This earlier horizon frames the first small crossings and visits that begin to make islands and straits historically active.

timeline.label: Neolithic Kythera
timeline.caption: Pottery scatters and obsidian place the island within a settled and connected Neolithic world.

timeline.label: Bronze Age Aegean networks
timeline.caption: Later maritime systems would intensify the corridor between the Peloponnese, Kythera, and Crete.

timeline.label: Early arrowhead on Antidragonera
timeline.caption: This tiny find marks a very early human presence in the wider Kytheran seascape.

paragraphs.text:
That is why this small patch of land serves as a fitting prelude to the early Mediterranean as a whole.
It brings together difficult landscapes, fragile local settlements, seaborne connection, ritual life, and repeated reoccupation over immense stretches of time.
It also reminds us that the Mediterranean was not born as a finished historical world.
It had to be made, slowly, through countless acts of movement, adaptation, and exchange.

figures.label: Figure 1.1
figures.caption: This panorama turns a small corner of Kythera into a Mediterranean miniature. It shows how one place can gather anchorage, movement, and repeated habitation into a single view.

timeline.label: Palaeolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: A very long human background before farming and before the sea became a dense medium of connection.

timeline.label: Neolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: Farming communities, island crossings, and small settled worlds begin to knit fragments together.

timeline.label: Bronze and Iron Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The sea becomes progressively more connected, institutionally complex, and historically legible.

paragraphs.text:
Three later arrivals on this same coast sharpen the warning.
Lord Elgin's shipwrecked cargo of marbles stands for the Western habit of seizing Mediterranean antiquity for its own purposes.
Gérard de Nerval's disappointed visit to Aphrodite's island stands for the tendency to romanticize the region and falsify it with fantasy.
The recent arrival of unnamed migrants from North Africa points to a third danger, the urge to avert our eyes from the parts of Mediterranean history that do not suit inherited cultural preferences.

timeline.label: European appropriation of Mediterranean antiquity
timeline.caption: The nineteenth century turned Mediterranean antiquity into an object of collection, removal, and romantic projection.

timeline.label: Contemporary Mediterranean migration
timeline.caption: Modern migration across the sea forms the later horizon behind the unnamed North African arrivals.

timeline.label: Wreck of the Mentor
timeline.caption: The loss of Elgin's ship stands for the modern seizure and relocation of Mediterranean antiquity.

timeline.label: Nerval on Kythera
timeline.caption: Nerval's visit turns the island into a test case for romantic projection and disappointment.

sections.title: Braudel, Connectivity, and the Corrupting Sea

paragraphs.text:
Any serious Mediterranean history begins under the shadow of Fernand Braudel.
He gave the sea itself pride of place, treated geography, economy, and culture as deeper forces than event politics, and taught historians to think in different scales of time.
His work made it possible to see the Mediterranean as a coherent field rather than a mere fringe of separate continents.

figures.label: Figure 1.2
figures.caption: Fernand Braudel, the great historian who taught readers to see the Mediterranean as a large and coherent field shaped by deep structures and long durations.

paragraphs.text:
More recently, Peregrine Horden and Nicholas Purcell pushed this vision further in The Corrupting Sea.
For them, the Mediterranean is shaped by three fundamentals.
Its landscapes are fragmented into innumerable micro-regions.
Life is governed by uncertainty, whether of rainfall, wind, harvest, earthquake, or eruption.
And the central sea makes movement and communication unusually easy, so that people can link fragments, redistribute risk, and seize opportunities.

From this combination arises a world of restless networks.
Mobility is not an optional extra but a condition of survival and advantage.
Communities, traders, migrants, raiders, patrons, and pilgrims all participate in shifting webs that expand, contract, and re-form without central design.
The Mediterranean is unified not by sameness, but by a patterned interplay of differences.
In that sense the sea corrupts.
It unsettles closed orders, disturbs self-sufficient systems, and repeatedly lets people, goods, and ideas slip across imposed boundaries.

Yet Horden and Purcell chiefly describe the Mediterranean of the first millennium BC and long after.
By then the sea had already become explicit to its inhabitants as a connected world, and ancient maps could place it at the center of the known lands.
The deeper problem is to understand how such a world came into being in the first place.

figures.label: Figure 1.3
figures.caption: An approximate map of the world as seen from a Mediterranean standpoint around 500 BC. Its value lies in showing the sea already imagined as a central organizing space.

timeline.label: Late Bronze Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: This is the important predecessor horizon before the basin was explicitly imagined as one connected sea.

timeline.label: First-millennium BC Mediterranean integration
timeline.caption: By this span the Mediterranean is increasingly traversed, named, and thought as a larger field.

timeline.label: Roman Mediterranean
timeline.caption: Rome gives one of the strongest later formulations of the sea as a single political world.

timeline.label: Hecataean Mediterranean map
timeline.caption: A Mediterranean-centered picture of the world makes the basin's conceptual centrality visible.

paragraphs.text:
The story cannot be told simply by starting with the Classical Mediterranean and rowing backward into earlier ages.
That would tempt us to pick out only those features that later became important, while ignoring the many paths that did not lead to the familiar world.
To understand the Mediterranean historically, one must ask when its characteristic patterns first emerged, and under what conditions they spread.

timeline.label: Neolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: One of the early horizons that would vanish from view if the story were told only backward from the Classical age.

timeline.label: Bronze Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: A major formative field whose internal developments cannot be reduced to later Classical outcomes.

timeline.label: Classical Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The familiar world from which one is tempted to row backward, thereby distorting the earlier record.

paragraphs.text:
This is especially important because the Mediterranean did not always exist in the full historical sense.
Until people could cross its waters with some confidence, the sea was not yet a medium of connection.
It was only a body of water.
What later became the Mediterranean world began as many separate streams of development, moving at different speeds and with different outcomes.
Sometimes they converged, sometimes they dried up, and often they produced emergent forms before anything like a full system appeared.

timeline.label: Palaeolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: People lived around the basin long before the sea functioned as a reliable medium of connection.

timeline.label: Mesolithic Mediterranean
timeline.caption: In this intermediate horizon, island crossings begin to matter more, even before the later dense networks of farming and metal-age exchange.

timeline.label: Connected Bronze and Iron Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: Only much later does the basin begin to resemble the historically connected Mediterranean familiar from written history.

paragraphs.text:
That early history matters for another reason as well.
It contains extraordinary human creativity within changing physical worlds.
It includes the emergence of our species, the spread of farming, the rise of navigation and exchange, the appearance of towns and states, and the growth of new habits of consumption, power, and belief.
It also matters because millions of people still invest this remote past with emotional and cultural significance in the present.

timeline.label: Homo sapiens in the Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The long human background in which our own species occupies the basin before farming.

timeline.label: Neolithic farming expansion
timeline.caption: Farming, new settlement patterns, and growing maritime links reshape Mediterranean life.

timeline.label: First towns and states
timeline.caption: Urban life, political concentration, and large-scale exchange become increasingly visible.

paragraphs.text:
For such remote periods, written evidence grows sparse and then disappears.
If the deeper Mediterranean is to be written as history, archaeology must carry much of the burden.
That means an archaeology willing to draw on every useful science, to move across immense spans of time, and to recover patterns of life from material traces rather than from texts alone.

sections.title: Archaeology, Scale, and a Barbarian History

paragraphs.text:
The difficulty is that Mediterranean archaeology has often become too specialized to sustain a wide view.
The flood of new data encourages narrow concentration on periods, regions, and techniques.
National and regional scholarship has also often preferred local trajectories, partly in reaction against older diffusionist habits that explained every major innovation as an import from Egypt or Mesopotamia.

A close regional focus has real value.
Without it, large-scale history becomes smooth and unreal.
Yet pushed too far, it produces intellectual parochialism.
One sees the small patch of sky perfectly and misses the constellations.
The task is therefore to connect local processes to larger structures without flattening either.

Genuinely pan-Mediterranean syntheses of the early basin remain rare.
David Trump provided one concise survey in 1980.
Braudel himself wrote a remarkable broad account of the ancient Mediterranean, though it remained unpublished for decades and was already dated in some of its assumptions.
Jean Guilaine carried the story powerfully through the Neolithic and early metal ages, but stopped before the whole arc had been completed.
The need for a new synthesis therefore remains pressing.

timeline.label: Late twentieth-century Mediterranean syntheses
timeline.caption: This short sequence marks the main modern attempts to recover a basin-wide early Mediterranean history.

timeline.label: Trump's Prehistory of the Mediterranean
timeline.caption: A concise synthetic account that helped define the problem.

timeline.label: Guilaine's La Mer Partagée
timeline.caption: A strong thematic treatment of Mediterranean societies up to the early second millennium BC.

timeline.label: Braudel's The Mediterranean in the Ancient World
timeline.caption: A posthumously published ancient-world synthesis by Braudel himself.

paragraphs.text:
Other approaches also leave something essential out.
Continental surveys divide the Mediterranean among Europe, Africa, and southwest Asia, and so break apart a world that often worked through the sea between them.
World-systems models, for all their value, can overemphasize impulses from the Near East and leave too much of the basin in shadow until those impulses arrive.
A truly Mediterranean history must be able to think both broadly and locally, by sea rather than by continental habit.

What is needed, then, is a barbarian history.
That does not mean neglecting the great societies of the eastern basin.
It means refusing to let Greek and Roman prestige predetermine the whole story.
The early Mediterranean was polyglot, uneven, and full of societies that do not exist merely as preludes to Classical Greece.
Even the Aegean should not be treated as though the Parthenon were already waiting at the starting line.

figures.label: Figure 1.4
figures.caption: An early first-millennium BC Sardinian bronze figurine recorded in an eighteenth-century engraving. It serves as a reminder that much of Mediterranean history lies outside the later Greek and Roman spotlight.

timeline.label: Early Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The broad field that this chapter insists must not be reduced to a prelude.

timeline.label: Archaic and Classical Greece
timeline.caption: The prestigious Aegean horizon that later historians too easily treat as the story's destination.

timeline.label: Roman Mediterranean
timeline.caption: A later imperial world that often overshadows the older and more plural Mediterranean.

paragraphs.text:
The Mediterranean is one of the richest regions in the world for early history, and one reason is simply the long and intense history of curiosity directed toward its remains.
Interest in old things there goes back to antiquity itself, but the modern story begins more clearly with Renaissance savants and the antiquaries of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

timeline.label: Ancient Mediterranean
timeline.caption: Curiosity about ruins and old things already belonged to the ancient world, long before archaeology became a discipline.

timeline.label: Renaissance antiquarian recovery
timeline.caption: Humanist scholarship begins to gather, compare, and value antiquities in a recognizably new way.

timeline.label: Antiquarian age
timeline.caption: Collectors and learned antiquaries prepare the ground for later archaeology.

paragraphs.text:
For a long time, Greek and Roman monuments dominated attention.
The Grand Tour, Neo-Classical taste, and the prestige of the classical past all encouraged collectors, excavators, and scholars to prize Mediterranean antiquities as trophies of civilization.
That legacy still matters.
Mediterranean archaeology remains unusually full of objects, museums, and beautiful survivals, and it has often been drawn toward possession, display, and admiration as much as explanation.

Even before formal prehistory took shape, scholars had begun to notice that some Mediterranean artifacts belonged to worlds older than Greece and Rome.
Stone tools, bronze figurines, and Egyptian monuments all widened the historical field.
Then, in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the study of the early Mediterranean expanded rapidly as archaeology, geology, and evolutionary thinking changed the scale of the human past.
This was also the age of the great excavations at sites such as Troy, Knossos, Ugarit, Jericho, and Thapsos.

timeline.label: Antiquarian recognition of pre-Classical objects
timeline.caption: Older artifacts begin to be noticed as belonging to worlds before Greece and Rome.

timeline.label: Formation of prehistoric archaeology
timeline.caption: Geology, evolution, and the new idea of prehistory reshape the scale of the human past.

timeline.label: Great excavation age
timeline.caption: Large Mediterranean digs make the early past newly visible on a heroic scale.

paragraphs.text:
Those famous digs transformed knowledge, but they were often rough by modern standards.
They exposed palaces, towns, cemeteries, and stratified tells on a heroic scale, yet they also destroyed information that would now be recovered with much greater care.
Figure 1.5 captures something of that older style.
It shows archaeology as spectacle, labor, and command, with heavy tools, large crews, and an almost theatrical confidence.

figures.label: Figure 1.5
figures.caption: A large early twentieth-century excavation at Ras Shamra. The image shows the older style of big dig, impressive in scale but far rougher in method than modern archaeology.

timeline.label: Great excavation age
timeline.caption: The old style of large, commanding excavations belongs chiefly to this phase.

timeline.label: Schliemann at Troy
timeline.caption: Troy becomes one of the emblematic early Mediterranean digs.

timeline.label: Evans at Knossos
timeline.caption: Knossos enters archaeology through a spectacular early twentieth-century excavation.

timeline.label: French mission at Ugarit
timeline.caption: Ras Shamra exemplifies the mature big-dig style captured in the figure.

paragraphs.text:
Much of this archaeology unfolded in colonial or quasi-colonial settings.
Before the Second World War, most Mediterranean archaeologists were foreign, often European, and they commonly worked within imperial structures or under strong foreign influence.
Yet the field was never made only by celebrated outsiders.
It also depended on local pioneers such as Christos Tsountas, Paolo Orsi, and Themistocles Zammit, whose work was often carried forward with fewer resources and far less glamour.
Figure 1.6 is a useful reminder of that indigenous strand.

figures.label: Figure 1.6
figures.caption: Themistocles Zammit, a central figure in Maltese archaeology. His presence helps correct the usual focus on foreign excavators by highlighting indigenous scholarship within the Mediterranean.

timeline.label: Colonial Mediterranean archaeology
timeline.caption: Much fieldwork in the basin took place under imperial or quasi-colonial conditions.

timeline.label: Levant mandate era
timeline.caption: After the First World War, archaeology in the eastern Mediterranean was folded into mandate politics.

timeline.label: Postwar decolonization
timeline.caption: This successor horizon transformed who excavated and under what political conditions.

paragraphs.text:
Since the nineteen fifties, the conditions of work have been transformed.
Archaeology across the Mediterranean has increasingly become national, institutional, and often tied to rescue work in advance of modern development.
There are now far more archaeologists, many more women, and much more fieldwork.
The result is not exhaustion but abundance.
New discoveries continue to widen the picture, while national and regional traditions have also given Mediterranean archaeology a greater intellectual diversity than before.

timeline.label: National archaeology after independence
timeline.caption: Archaeology increasingly becomes national, institutional, and locally administered.

timeline.label: Rescue archaeology expansion
timeline.caption: Modern development drives a dramatic growth of salvage and preventive excavation.

timeline.label: Plural Mediterranean archaeology
timeline.caption: The field becomes larger, more diverse, and intellectually less dependent on older outside centers.

paragraphs.text:
The Mediterranean is also favored by an unusual range of preservation conditions.
Most archaeological records survive only as thin residues left after decay, breakage, reuse, and loss.
Here, however, nature sometimes grants startling exceptions.
Waterlogging, aridity, volcanic ash, and even ice can preserve whole capsules of ancient life and force us to abandon overly minimal views of the past.

Shipwrecks and drowned settlements preserve waterlogged worlds.
Dry caves in Israel, southern Spain, and the Balearics keep fragile materials that would vanish elsewhere.
Volcanic destruction created Bronze Age sites of astonishing completeness.
At Akrotiri on Thera, whole buildings survived beneath ash, while at Croce del Papa near Vesuvius even huts and trapped animals were preserved.
Figures 1.7 and 1.8 show how dramatically such conditions can enlarge the evidence.

figures.label: Figure 1.7
figures.caption: Waterlogged wooden structures at La Draga in Catalonia. The site shows how unusual preservation can recover fragile parts of ancient life that normally disappear.

figures.label: Figure 1.8
figures.caption: Akrotiri on Thera preserved beneath volcanic deposits. The image makes clear how ash can freeze an entire Bronze Age town in startling detail.

timeline.label: Neolithic drowned settlements
timeline.caption: Waterlogged coastal settings preserve early villages and wooden structures that are usually lost.

timeline.label: Bronze Age Mediterranean towns
timeline.caption: This broader horizon contains the urban and proto-urban settings preserved by unusual catastrophe.

timeline.label: Late Bronze Age Aegean eruption horizon
timeline.caption: A narrower volcanic horizon frames Akrotiri and the dramatic preservation of Thera.

timeline.label: Akrotiri eruption horizon
timeline.caption: The burial of Akrotiri beneath volcanic deposits created one of the great preserved Bronze Age time capsules.

paragraphs.text:
Texts and images add another kind of richness, though not without strict limits.
Writing appears first in the eastern Mediterranean and the Aegean, not across the whole basin, and some scripts remain undeciphered.
Even where writing survives, it is uneven in subject matter and social reach.
The Aegean tablets are mostly administrative.
In the east, written evidence soon ranges more widely across diplomacy, religion, law, royal display, and economic life.

timeline.label: Early eastern Mediterranean writing
timeline.caption: Writing first takes root in the eastern literate worlds rather than across the whole basin.

timeline.label: Aegean scripts
timeline.caption: The Aegean enters the written world later and more narrowly than the Levant and Egypt.

timeline.label: First-millennium Mediterranean alphabets
timeline.caption: Writing becomes far more widely distributed around the basin in later periods.

paragraphs.text:
Yet texts are invaluable when handled with care.
They were not written for our convenience, and they often tell us as much about ideology and habit as about events.
Ramesses the Second could nearly lose a battle and still proclaim victory on stone.
But inscriptions, archives, and records can also reveal marriage politics, luxury values, production systems, and the submerged assumptions of ancient elites.
Figure 1.9 makes the abundance of such written archives in parts of the eastern Mediterranean strikingly visible.

figures.label: Figure 1.9
figures.caption: Clay tablets from the archive of Ebla. They demonstrate the extraordinary density of written evidence available in some eastern Mediterranean settings.

timeline.label: Ebla archive horizon
timeline.caption: One of the great early eastern archives, showing how dense written evidence can become.

timeline.label: New Kingdom Egypt
timeline.caption: The Egyptian imperial world provides the context for Ramesses the Second and his inscriptions.

timeline.label: Battle of Qadesh
timeline.caption: A famous case in which royal inscriptional triumph outruns the likely military reality.

paragraphs.text:
Images deserve the same double response.
They are more widely distributed than texts, but they too must be read with caution.
They do not simply hand the past over to us.
They record ancient ways of seeing, selecting, and ordering, and their value lies partly in learning how to read those habits without mistaking them for transparent windows.

sections.title: Excavation, Survey, and the Underwater Frontier

paragraphs.text:
Excavation remains central, but its form has changed.
The enormous dig of an earlier age has become rarer because careful recovery, recording, analysis, and publication are now far slower and more expensive.
Where large excavations still continue, they usually depend on exceptional funding or national prestige.
Even so, one should not forget what is lost when truly major sites can only be sampled in fragments.

At the same time, archaeology has gained by turning more seriously toward small sites and rescue digs.
Rural settlements, caves, ditches, and other modest traces have widened the questions that can be asked.
Work done ahead of roads, housing estates, and other construction has revealed entire classes of settlements that were once barely visible.
Figure 1.10 shows one such case, where the plan of a modern development overlies the remains of a large Neolithic village.

figures.label: Figure 1.10
figures.caption: Rescue archaeology at Villeneuve-Tolosane reveals a large Neolithic settlement beneath a modern housing layout. It shows how development-led excavation can uncover entire hidden landscapes.

paragraphs.text:
Surface survey has been just as transformative.
Instead of concentrating only on a few famous ruins, archaeologists now comb whole landscapes and track changing activity across valleys, islands, plains, cities, and uplands.
This method has turned apparent emptiness into inhabited terrain.
It has shown how densely Mediterranean countrysides could be filled with hamlets, work areas, paths, and shifting patterns of use.
Figure 1.11 returns us to Kythera and to the patient, close walking that makes such lost landscapes reappear.

figures.label: Figure 1.11
figures.caption: Archaeologists surveying the uplands of Kythera. The image captures the slow, systematic walking that turns an apparently empty landscape into a dense record of past activity.

timeline.label: Early landscape survey
timeline.caption: The first large reconnaissance surveys begin to move archaeology beyond a few famous ruins.

timeline.label: Intensive surface survey
timeline.caption: Closely spaced walking and denser collection radically enlarge what can be seen in a landscape.

timeline.label: Kythera survey season
timeline.caption: The fieldwork on Kythera belongs to the mature intensive-survey tradition.

paragraphs.text:
Survey also matters because it gives some sense of scale.
Without rough estimates of how many people lived in a region, and how populations rose or collapsed, history easily loses proportion.
For much of the Mediterranean past, especially outside the range of written fiscal records, those estimates depend on the number, size, and distribution of sites traced across the land.

timeline.label: Last Glacial Maximum
timeline.caption: At the glacial peak, Mediterranean population may have been extremely sparse.

timeline.label: Postglacial and Neolithic demographic recovery
timeline.caption: Population begins to recover as climates ease and farming spreads.

timeline.label: Roman imperial Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The later Roman horizon stands at the opposite extreme of demographic concentration and documentary visibility.

paragraphs.text:
A further frontier lies underwater.
Maritime archaeology has long been one of the Mediterranean's most exciting strengths, from the early shipwreck excavations off the Turkish coast to newer work in deep water.
The Uluburun wreck revealed a cargo of extraordinary range and complexity.
Now remote technologies are extending research far below ordinary diving depth and opening the possibility of finding ancient open-sea wrecks preserved from casual disturbance.
Figure 1.12 belongs to that frontier.

figures.label: Figure 1.12
figures.caption: A diver raising cargo from the Uluburun wreck off southern Turkey. The scene represents the underwater frontier of Mediterranean archaeology and the recovery of long-distance maritime connections.

timeline.label: Late Bronze Age seafaring
timeline.caption: The great wrecks belong to a mature phase of eastern Mediterranean maritime exchange.

timeline.label: Uluburun wreck
timeline.caption: This wreck offers an extraordinarily rich picture of long-distance cargo and shipboard life.

timeline.label: Cape Gelidonya wreck
timeline.caption: An early landmark in underwater excavation and a key wreck of the late Bronze Age.

paragraphs.text:
Underwater archaeology is not only about ships.
It also includes drowned villages, submerged caves, and ancient harbors reconstructed through coring and coastal study.
Taken together, these lines of inquiry help recover the maritime dimension without which Mediterranean history would scarcely make sense.

timeline.label: Postglacial sea-level rise
timeline.caption: Rising seas drowned caves, villages, and coastal settings around the Mediterranean.

timeline.label: Cosquer cave last dry access
timeline.caption: The cave was last entered on foot before postglacial waters sealed it away.

timeline.label: Deep-water cargo ships off Israel
timeline.caption: These wrecks show that deep-water maritime archaeology is beginning to reach very early open-sea traffic.

timeline.label: Deep-water merchantman off Cyprus
timeline.caption: A later deep-water find shows how far below normal diving range early shipping can now be traced.

paragraphs.text:
A final frontier lies in archaeological science.
The Mediterranean has become a privileged zone for many scientific techniques.
They can identify the origin of materials, reconstruct ancient technologies, detect residues in pottery, recover environmental evidence, and read life histories from bones and teeth.
Obsidian can sometimes be traced to its geological source.
Pottery fabrics can reveal where containers were made.
Organic residues can hint at oils, resins, alcohols, or foods once held in vessels.

Other methods widen the field still further.
Environmental archaeology studies seeds, pollen, charcoal, phytoliths, and animal bones in order to reconstruct diet, domestication, landscape, and economy.
Bioarchaeological work on skeletons can reveal health, labor, trauma, diet, and mobility.
Genetic evidence has drawn particular attention, though it must be handled with caution, especially when patterns in living populations are projected backward into deep time.

All of this has immense power, but science does not relieve archaeology of interpretation.
It is one thing to show that a material moved from one place to another.
It is another to explain why anyone wanted it, how it was acquired, what it was worth, who controlled it, and what social meaning it carried when it arrived.
Those larger questions return us to human motives, institutions, and habits.
Science sharpens the evidence.
It does not abolish the need for historical imagination.

sections.title: North Africa and the Southern Gap

paragraphs.text:
The riches of Mediterranean archaeology are real, but they are very unevenly distributed.
Some gaps are minor and will gradually be filled.
Others are more serious.
One gap, however, is so large that it threatens the balance of the whole field.

That gap lies in Mediterranean North Africa.
Minor shortages of evidence can be found in parts of Turkey, the southern Balkans, Albania, the former Yugoslavia, and Lebanon.
But west of Egypt, the dearth of information on early societies is of another order altogether.
It leaves the southern shore dangerously underrepresented in any account of the early Mediterranean.

The contrast is striking because Africa lies so near.
Saharan dust can drift north across the narrow middle sea and fall as red rain on Sicily, southern Italy, and even Greece.
Figure 1.13 captures that physical closeness.
Yet in most modern writing, the southern flank from the late Palaeolithic to Phoenician and Greek settlement is still treated almost as a blank.

figures.label: Figure 1.13
figures.caption: A plume of Saharan dust drifting north across the central Mediterranean. The image makes the physical closeness of Africa to southern Europe vivid, even where archaeology often leaves the southern shore obscure.

timeline.label: Late Palaeolithic North Africa
timeline.caption: The southern shore is visible here, but later long spans remain poorly documented.

timeline.label: Phoenician settlement horizon
timeline.caption: By this horizon, the southern Mediterranean re-enters many narratives more clearly.

timeline.label: Greek Cyrenaica
timeline.caption: Greek settlement in Cyrenaica is one of the later eastern openings through which North Africa becomes more legible.

paragraphs.text:
This neglect is disastrous for any serious Mediterranean history.
The fertile belt from Tunisia to the Atlantic makes up roughly a quarter of the basin's land.
The coast from Alexandria to Ceuta forms a major share of its shoreline.
Whether this region followed the same rhythms as the rest of the basin or moved to a different pattern, its history cannot simply be skipped.

The problem is not merely that nobody looked.
Under colonial rule a fair amount of archaeology was done in the Maghreb, and Gabriel Camps became an especially forceful defender of North African archaeology and Berber culture.
In Cyrenaica, British excavators opened the vast cave of Haua Fteah in the nineteen fifties and exposed a sequence running from the Palaeolithic to the Greek period.
Figure 1.14 shows that great cavern, which still anchors the deep chronology of much of North Africa.

figures.label: Figure 1.14
figures.caption: The vast cave of Haua Fteah in Cyrenaica during excavation. It remains one of the key deep sequences for North African prehistory from the Palaeolithic to the Greek period.

timeline.label: North African Palaeolithic
timeline.caption: Haua Fteah matters because it preserves a very long prehistoric sequence on the southern shore.

timeline.label: Epipalaeolithic and Neolithic North Africa
timeline.caption: The cave bridges the long transition from late foraging worlds toward later settled horizons.

timeline.label: Greek Cyrenaica
timeline.caption: Its sequence reaches down toward the historical horizon of Greek settlement in Cyrenaica.

paragraphs.text:
Earlier scholarship also spent much energy on supposed links across the sea.
Some scholars imagined lost land bridges between Africa and Europe.
Others even proposed that important cultural impulses had moved from the Maghreb northward.
When those theories were discredited in the nineteen thirties, chronology became sounder, but the intellectual bond between the two shores weakened as well.

Political independence then changed the field again.
Foreign archaeologists became fewer, especially in Algeria, and many of those who remained concentrated either on human origins or on the grand Roman and later remains.
Archaeology, burdened by its colonial past and competing with urgent modern priorities, struggled to become deeply rooted in local institutions.
Recent work in Tunisia, Libya, and Morocco offers some encouragement, but compared with the rapid advances elsewhere in the Mediterranean, knowledge of the early southern flank west of Egypt has barely moved.

timeline.label: North African independence wave
timeline.caption: Political independence reshaped who excavated, funded, and interpreted the region's past.

timeline.label: Algerian independence
timeline.caption: This was the climactic and bloodily contested turning point in the decolonization of the Maghreb.

timeline.label: Postcolonial archaeological slowdown
timeline.caption: In much of Mediterranean North Africa, early-period archaeology failed to accelerate as it did elsewhere.

paragraphs.text:
Even so, the silence of the record may not be explained by neglect alone.
There are signs that parts of Mediterranean North Africa followed a different trajectory from the northern and eastern shores.
In Tunisia, recent survey has found very few sites older than the first millennium BC, even in areas that are otherwise well prospected.
That meagerness is so stark that it suggests not just missing evidence, but another historical pattern.

timeline.label: Pre-first-millennium BC North Africa
timeline.caption: The striking scarcity of sites from this long span is one of the chapter's central puzzles.

timeline.label: Phoenician and Greek settlement horizon
timeline.caption: This is the later threshold after which the southern shore becomes easier to see in many narratives.

timeline.label: Roman North Africa
timeline.caption: By contrast, Roman-era site density in Tunisia is immensely more visible.

paragraphs.text:
One plausible explanation is that much of the North African littoral long faced south rather than north.
People may have been oriented toward hunting, gathering, and later pastoral movement across the continental interior rather than toward maritime exchange within the Mediterranean.
Geography may have reinforced this.
A rugged mountain rim faced the sea, currents could be adverse, and the Sahara broke habitable zones into something like widely separated coastal islands.

timeline.label: Hunter-gatherer North Africa
timeline.caption: One possible southern trajectory centers on wild-resource use rather than early maritime entanglement.

timeline.label: Saharan pastoral horizon
timeline.caption: Mobile herding links Mediterranean Africa strongly to inland African worlds.

timeline.label: Phoenician and Greek maritime world
timeline.caption: This external horizon sharpens the contrast with a more south-facing North African trajectory.

paragraphs.text:
This does not make Mediterranean Africa less historical.
It means that its history may have been woven into larger African worlds as much as into the sea to its north.
To understand the early Mediterranean properly, one must sometimes move further into Africa rather than less.
The southern shore cannot be restored to the story merely by treating it as a weaker copy of the Levant or Europe.

Egypt presents a different version of the same difficulty.
The Nile Delta is no neglected backwater, but much of its early archaeology lies buried beneath thick river silt and often below the water table.
That makes both discovery and excavation difficult.
Only a few windows have opened since the nineteen eighties, yet even these suggest that Delta communities could look very different from those of the Nile Valley and could stand closer to their Mediterranean neighbors.
Any Mediterranean history of Egypt must therefore look at the country through this deltaic junction as well as through the long river corridor to the south.

sections.title: New Frameworks of Time and Climate

paragraphs.text:
One of the great structural revolutions in early Mediterranean archaeology was chronological.
Radiocarbon dating made it possible to build stand alone time frames for every part of the basin and to set local sequences within an absolute calendar.
Before that, much of the chronology had been tied, directly or indirectly, to Egyptian kings and to fragile chains of stylistic comparison.

timeline.label: Egyptian-based chronological framework
timeline.caption: For a long time Mediterranean chronology depended on Egyptian king lists and stylistic chains.

timeline.label: Radiocarbon revolution
timeline.caption: Radiocarbon dating begins to give every region an independent absolute timescale.

timeline.label: Calibrated radiocarbon era
timeline.caption: Calibration and refinement make the resulting chronological grid far more trustworthy.

paragraphs.text:
The consequences were immense.
Calibrated radiocarbon dates lengthened many chronologies and altered key synchronisms.
Phenomena once treated as delayed echoes of the east turned out to be earlier than expected or fully independent.
The great temples of Malta and some of the first megalithic tombs in the western Mediterranean, for example, proved to be older than the pyramids rather than imitations of them.

timeline.label: Western Mediterranean megalithic horizon
timeline.caption: Megalithic tombs in the west belong to a long local tradition rather than a late eastern echo.

timeline.label: Maltese Temple period
timeline.caption: The great Maltese temples belong to a very early monumental horizon in the central Mediterranean.

timeline.label: Egyptian pyramid age
timeline.caption: The pyramids remain a major eastern landmark, but not the universal starting point once imagined.

paragraphs.text:
Radiocarbon also pushed secure dating far deeper into the past.
It opened a time scale that reaches tens of thousands of years before the first pharaohs.
Later refinements, together with tree ring dating and other methods, now allow most of the early Mediterranean to be discussed in calendrical BC terms.
There are still serious arguments over some fine points, especially in the second millennium BC Aegean, but the larger chronological framework has been transformed.

timeline.label: Deep prehistoric Mediterranean
timeline.caption: Radiocarbon dating opens a secure chronology for periods far older than writing or dynasties.

timeline.label: Neolithic and Bronze Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The long middle stretch of Mediterranean prehistory can now be placed on an absolute timescale.

timeline.label: Pharaonic Egypt
timeline.caption: The older chronological system had leaned heavily on dynastic Egypt before scientific dating widened the frame.

paragraphs.text:
That transformation did more than correct dates.
It freed the central and western Mediterranean from an old habit that treated eastern priority as the default explanation for every major development.
It also helps loosen the grip of the inherited labels that have too often cramped interpretation.
Once chronology is better founded, historical periods can be used more critically rather than repeated as fixed containers.

A second and still unfolding revolution concerns climate change.
The Mediterranean of the Pleistocene was plainly not the Mediterranean of today, and even the Holocene has been far from stable.
Research now draws on marine cores, ice cores, lake beds, pollen, shorelines, tree rings, cave deposits, and many other proxies.
Figure 1.15 brings several of these climate records into a single frame and makes their jagged variability hard to ignore.

figures.label: Figure 1.15
figures.caption: Several climate records from around and beyond the Mediterranean set side by side. Their similar jagged patterns show that large environmental shifts were frequent and that the basin must be read within wider climatic change.

timeline.label: Late Pleistocene
timeline.caption: The Mediterranean of the ice age differed radically from the basin familiar today.

timeline.label: Holocene
timeline.caption: The present interglacial is calmer than the Pleistocene, but far from uniform.

timeline.label: Little Ice Age
timeline.caption: A well-known later oscillation reminds us that climate variation continued even within historic times.

paragraphs.text:
The broad lesson is that change has been normal.
The tempo could be rapid, and even the relatively calm Holocene contains wetter phases, drier phases, medium term oscillations, and a few severe short term events.
The environmental conditions that later made the Mediterranean seem like a naturally fragmented and uncertain world were not eternal.
They belong to a particular span within a much longer history of shifting regimes.

timeline.label: Early Holocene humid phase
timeline.caption: A wetter predecessor regime shaped the basin very differently from later Mediterranean conditions.

timeline.label: Late Holocene Mediterranean regime
timeline.caption: The familiar fragmented and uncertain Mediterranean belongs mainly to this long but not eternal phase.

timeline.label: Modern warming transition
timeline.caption: The basin is now entering another environmental regime whose consequences are still unfolding.

paragraphs.text:
This does not mean that every coincidence between climate and human history proves causation.
Yet it does mean that climate can no longer be treated as a decorative backdrop.
It must be brought into the center of Mediterranean history as one active element among others.
The difficulty is to do so without collapsing into determinism.

Climate does not dictate one necessary human response.
Its effects depend on speed, scale, duration, and frequency, and also on what people perceive as danger or opportunity.
A drought might ruin one community and strengthen another if control of food, labor, or ritual gives some groups unusual leverage.
Environmental strain can provoke innovation, migration, conflict, intensified religion, or collapse, and neighboring societies may respond in very different ways.

One final caution runs in the opposite direction.
As attention to environmental pressure has become more subtle, older claims about catastrophic human destruction of Mediterranean environments have begun to look too simple.
There are a few serious cases, but not many.
The deeper lesson is that neither climate nor human agency should be turned into a single master key.
The history of the Mediterranean was shaped by changing environments, but always through the selective responses of human societies.

The early Mediterranean survives in one of the worst possible places for long term preservation.
Its archaeological wealth lies across countries that are often economically strained and heavily pressed by modern demands.
For that reason, the past needs defenders no less urgently than the coastlines, wetlands, and landscapes around it.

The most universal danger comes from development.
Modern farming in long occupied lowlands has already destroyed countless sites without record.
Urban growth continues over ancient centers, while mass tourism drives relentless construction along beaches, harbors, and coastal roads.
Figure 1.16 makes that pressure visible in the built up coastline of southern Spain.

figures.label: Figure 1.16
figures.caption: Heavy development along the coast at Torremolinos in southern Spain. The image shows how mass tourism and construction can overwhelm both the shoreline and the archaeological record.

paragraphs.text:
These pressures fall most heavily on the narrow zone where land meets sea.
That coastal membrane is also where the struggle over pollution, sustainability, and ecological damage is most intense.
Archaeology cannot defend itself there in isolation.
It has to make common cause with wider movements for conservation of landscape and water.

The scale of the pressure is hard to overstate.
Large stretches of the Mediterranean coast now lie under concrete or tarmac.
Some islands receive numbers of visitors that far exceed their own populations.
Tourism may prevent abandonment and sustain local incomes, but it also accelerates the destruction of fragile settings that took millennia to form.

In such circumstances, even rescue archaeology can feel like a losing battle.
When a famous site is at stake, public attention may secure planning, funding, and careful visitor management.
At Hal Saflieni on Malta, for example, access has been tightly controlled in order to preserve a highly vulnerable underground complex.
Figure 1.18 shows that kind of deliberate management at work.

figures.label: Figure 1.18
figures.caption: Carefully managed access at the underground complex of Hal Saflieni on Malta. The arrangement shows how fragile sites can survive only through strict control, infrastructure, and public planning.

timeline.label: Maltese Temple period
timeline.caption: Hal Saflieni belongs to the same broad monumental culture as prehistoric Malta's great temples.

timeline.label: Saflieni phase
timeline.caption: The hypogeum itself belongs within this narrower prehistoric horizon.

timeline.label: Later Maltese prehistory
timeline.caption: This successor span helps place the site within a longer island sequence rather than as an isolated monument.

paragraphs.text:
Far more often, however, the threatened place is little known, newly found, or judged expendable.
Then the struggle may be only to document it before bulldozers arrive.
What is hardest of all to preserve is not a single monument but a whole landscape, such as a city with its cemeteries, or a sanctuary within its broader setting.

The fate of Beirut after the civil war shows how severe the loss can be.
During reconstruction, huge areas of the historic core were cleared without proper archaeological supervision.
Map 1.17 makes the imbalance stark.
Large zones were rebuilt after excavation, but much else was destroyed with barely any record at all.

figures.label: Map 1.17
figures.caption: Central Beirut after the civil war, with zones excavated, zones bulldozed without archaeology, and areas where archaeologists came only after destruction. The map shows how rebuilding can preserve some memory while erasing far more.

timeline.label: Ancient and medieval Beirut
timeline.caption: The city whose layers were endangered in reconstruction had accumulated a very long urban history.

timeline.label: Lebanese civil war
timeline.caption: The war forms the immediate background to the destruction and rebuilding of central Beirut.

timeline.label: Postwar reconstruction
timeline.caption: It was during reconstruction that much of the archaeological record was cleared or lost.

paragraphs.text:
This kind of erasure is not only physical.
It is a destruction of memory in a city already struggling to remember itself.
What rises afterward may look new and prosperous, yet be severed from the strata that once gave it depth.
A rebuilt city can become, in effect, a phoenix that has forgotten its own life before the fire.

A second danger comes from looting for the art market.
Classical material has often suffered most, but older things have been plundered on a vast scale as well.
Cycladic marble figurines, Sardinian bronzes, and almost any object that can be sold for cash are drawn into this trade.
Figure 1.19 stands for that mutilation of context.

figures.label: Figure 1.19
figures.caption: Fragments of Cycladic marble figurines dispersed after looting from Keros. Their beauty survives, but the archaeological setting that would have explained them has been broken apart.

timeline.label: Cycladic figurine horizon
timeline.caption: The looted marble figures belong to the early Bronze Age Cyclades.

timeline.label: Nuragic and early Iron Age Sardinia
timeline.caption: Sardinian bronzes show that the trade reaches far beyond the Greek and Roman world.

timeline.label: Modern antiquities market
timeline.caption: The ancient objects now circulate within a much later market of collectors, dealers, and museums.

paragraphs.text:
Looting does not merely remove beautiful objects.
It kills history by stripping things away from the settings that made them intelligible.
Once tombs, shrines, or settlement layers have been ransacked, the surviving objects become isolated trophies and the site itself is often ruined beyond repair.
What is sold abroad is therefore only the visible fragment of a much larger destruction.

Poverty at the source helps sustain this trade, but the problem does not end there.
As long as collectors, dealers, and museums continue to desire objects of dubious origin, the incentive remains.
Real change will require pressure not only on those who dig illegally, but also on those who buy, display, and legitimize what has been stolen.
The market is not an aftereffect of looting.
It is one of its causes.

sections.title: The Past, Identity, and the Mediterranean Future

paragraphs.text:
The early Mediterranean matters not only because its remains are threatened, but because its past is constantly drawn into present struggles.
That use is almost inevitable.
The deeper the past, the easier it is to bend toward imperial dreams, national myths, or sectarian claims.

The modern Mediterranean is no peaceful museum.
Its recent history includes civil wars, occupations, expulsions, divided islands, refugees at sea, and economies under intense strain.
Figure 1.20, with refugees crowded on a small boat bound for Lampedusa, shows that the sea is still a passage of risk, desperation, and unequal hope.

figures.label: Figure 1.20
figures.caption: North African refugees crowded onto a small boat reaching Lampedusa. The scene shows that the Mediterranean is still a corridor of dangerous movement, not merely a setting for leisure.

paragraphs.text:
In such a world, the past becomes politically useful.
Rulers, empires, colonial administrations, provinces, and nation states have all pressed archaeology into service.
Ancient places can be used to justify conquest, deepen local loyalties, weaken rival affiliations, or give new states a more ancient pedigree.
The distance of the past from the present is precisely what makes it so easy to manipulate.

Such manipulation has taken many forms.
Colonial powers could foster local archaeological identities in order to distract from more dangerous solidarities.
National movements could elevate one ancient inheritance above all others.
Regional movements could turn old monuments into emblems of autonomy or grievance.
The Mediterranean has repeatedly used antiquity as a language for present ambitions.

For that reason, archaeology cannot withdraw from public debate without betraying part of its task.
It has to challenge crude uses of the past and to show that older societies were rarely as simple, pure, or neatly bounded as political myth prefers.
A more accurate history does not erase attachment.
It makes attachment less violent and less false.

The word Mediterranean itself is not innocent.
To some it suggests cosmopolitan exchange, openness, and relief from narrow national identities.
To others it sounds like an outsider's stereotype, romantic when flattering and contemptuous when dismissive.
The same term can mean blue skies and hospitality, or corruption, weakness, and the need for external control.

Yet those competing meanings also reveal a desire for wider forms of belonging.
Some invoke the Mediterranean to escape confinement within the nation.
Others use it to mark distance from surrounding continental worlds.
No single usage can claim final authority.
What matters is that the term continues to invite thought about connections larger than the state and older than modern borders.

A long view of the early Mediterranean can contribute something valuable here.
It uncovers a world before monotheistic rivalry hardened the basin in later forms, and before national identities claimed to reach unchanged into remote antiquity.
That older world was not simple harmony.
It was a dense tapestry of shifting practices, contacts, and partial identities.

timeline.label: Polytheistic Bronze and Iron Age Mediterranean
timeline.caption: The long pre-monotheistic Mediterranean provides the wider field this paragraph wants to recover.

timeline.label: Mediterranean monotheisms and late antiquity
timeline.caption: Later religious hardening belongs to a very different basin from the earlier one.

timeline.label: Modern Mediterranean nation-states
timeline.caption: Modern national claims to remote antiquity are a much later overlay on the older world.

paragraphs.text:
As soon as texts and images become plentiful, one already finds peoples being represented as different, inferior, or threatening.
Figure 1.21 shows this clearly in Egyptian royal art, where foreigners are displayed beneath the king's power.
But such images do not prove that the ancient Mediterranean was naturally divided into fixed and eternal blocks.
They show, rather, how early and how forcefully human beings tried to impose such blocks.

figures.label: Figure 1.21
figures.caption: Egyptian royal art depicting Levantines, Nubians, and Libyans beneath Ramesses the Second. It is a vivid example of how ancient power used visual stereotypes to define outsiders.

timeline.label: New Kingdom Egypt
timeline.caption: The depiction of foreigners belongs to the imperial horizon of New Kingdom Egypt.

timeline.label: Ramesses the Second
timeline.caption: His reign is the specific royal frame for the image discussed here.

timeline.label: Later Iron Age Mediterranean identities
timeline.caption: Later ethnic and political identities become more explicit, but they do not simply confirm the older Egyptian stereotypes.

paragraphs.text:
The deeper reality is more fluid.
Communities, customs, and affiliations were continually made and remade through interaction.
The solid groups and boundaries inherited by later ages emerged only gradually, often late, and under pressures that can still be studied.
The early Mediterranean is therefore not a gallery of ready made nations.
It is a field of movement, convergence, friction, and recombination.

That vision can itself become too easy if turned into a cheerful celebration of mixture.
Mediterraneanization, if one may call it that, created winners and losers as well as connections.
Every widening network altered balances of power and left some people marginalized, displaced, or absorbed on unequal terms.
A history of interaction that forgets this becomes as false as the nationalist stories it was meant to replace.

Even so, the basin remains one of the best places in which to study how human worlds are made through mobility, encounter, imitation, resistance, and conflict.
Its early history does not offer a simple lesson or a ready cure for the present.
What it offers is a broader and more demanding perspective.
To ignore that past is to become poorer in judgment, and perhaps less capable of imagining a livable future around this sea.
